## Rule to apply

- Use the **5-point individual threshold** at cycle boundary.
- If a person is carrying **5 points or less** of unfinished estimated work, keep it attached to the original item and re-plan it in the next cycle as-is.
- If a person is carrying **more than 5 points** of unfinished estimated work, the lead must split the leftover work before next-cycle planning starts.

- Identify every platform item that is not done by the end of the current cycle.
- For each unfinished item, confirm what work is actually complete versus still remaining.

- Check the remaining work by individual owner, not only by ticket.

- Keep only one slice tied to the carryover item if needed; create separate follow-up slices for the rest.
- Make each split slice independently reviewable, demoable, or releasable where possible.
- Move blocked or dependency-heavy work into its own slice so it does not hide the shippable portion.
- Reassign owners only if capacity has actually changed; do not use reassignment to avoid the threshold rule.
- In the planning doc, note for each carryover item: original estimate, completed portion, remaining estimate, and the split plan.
- Confirm the total carried-in work still fits next-cycle team capacity before adding new commitments.

- Original item: `Harden cluster rollout automation`, estimated at `8 points`, owned by one engineer.
- Completed this cycle: `3 points` worth of work.

- `Carryover rule: use the 5-point individual threshold; any unfinished remaining work above 5 points for one person must be split before next-cycle commitment.`

# Standup Rhythm

## Overview

The org does not run live daily standups. Daily standups have been canceled and replaced with daily written status posts.

Our rhythm is simple:

- Every weekday: post a written status update.
- Once each week: join the shared org gathering.

This keeps day-to-day communication lightweight while still giving the company one live moment each week to stay aligned.

## Weekly Pattern

### Monday Through Friday

Every team member posts one written status update each workday.

Use your daily post to answer three questions:

1. What did I complete since my last update?
2. What am I focused on today?
3. What is blocked, at risk, or needs help?

Keep the update short and readable. In most cases, 3 to 6 bullets is enough.

### Weekly Shared Gathering

The org has one shared live gathering each week.

This is the only recurring company-wide sync in the standup rhythm. It is not a replacement for daily written updates, and it does not eliminate the expectation to post your normal written status on that day.

Use the shared gathering for:

- cross-org visibility
- major updates worth hearing live
- risks or dependencies that affect multiple teams
- brief recognition or celebration

## What Participation Looks Like

### On Ordinary Days

On a normal workday, participation means:

1. Read recent updates that affect your work.
2. Post your own written status update.
3. Call out blockers clearly and tag the people or teams who may need to respond.
4. Update your post if priorities change in a meaningful way.

If your work is steady and there are no blockers, a concise update is the right update.

### On the Shared Gathering Day

Participation means:

1. Post your written status update as usual.
2. Join the live org gathering.
3. Come prepared to share only information that is useful at org scope.
4. Keep live updates brief and focused on decisions, dependencies, risks, and outcomes.

The weekly gathering is for shared awareness. Detailed project discussion should move to the right follow-up thread or meeting.

## Writing a Good Daily Status Post

A strong update is:

- specific
- concise
- current
- action-oriented

Include concrete progress, the next step, and any blocker early. If you need help, say exactly what is needed and from whom.

Example:

> Completed onboarding flow QA and merged the copy fixes.  
> Today I am validating analytics events in production.  
> Blocked on access to the billing dashboard from Finance.

If you are new to the company, follow this default:

1. Post one written status update every workday.
2. Do this even on the day of the weekly shared gathering.
3. Join the weekly shared gathering unless you are out of office or have an approved conflict.
4. Ask for help in the written update as soon as a blocker appears; do not wait for the live gathering.

When in doubt, optimize for clarity and consistency. A short daily post on time is better than a perfect update posted late.

# Org Standup Rhythm

Our org runs standups on a simple weekly cadence: four async check-ins and one shared live gathering.

## Weekly Pattern

| Day | Format | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | Async | Post your standup update in the org standup channel by 12:00 p.m. local time |
| Tuesday | Async | Post your standup update in the org standup channel by 12:00 p.m. local time |
| Wednesday | Live | Join the shared org standup and give a brief verbal update |
| Thursday | Async | Post your standup update in the org standup channel by 12:00 p.m. local time |
| Friday | Async | Post your standup update in the org standup channel by 12:00 p.m. local time |

That means the default rhythm is async on ordinary workdays, with Wednesday as the one day the org meets together live.

## Async Days

On Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday, everyone who is working that day posts one async update.

Keep it short and specific. Each update should cover these three points:

1. What you finished since your last update
2. What you are working on next
3. Any blocker, dependency, or decision you need help with

Aim for 3 to 6 sentences total. Link to tickets, docs, or threads when that gives helpful context. If you do not have blockers, say `No blockers`.

## Wednesday Shared Gathering

Wednesday is the one shared live standup for the org.

Come ready to cover the same three points you use in async updates:

1. What you finished
2. What you are doing next
3. What needs support or attention

Keep your verbal update to about 30 to 60 seconds. The goal is to surface priorities, unblock cross-functional work, and share context that is faster to align on live than in text.

## Participation Expectations

- Participate every workday unless you are out of office
- Post exactly one async update on each async day you are working
- Attend the Wednesday live standup unless you are out of office or have a scheduling conflict
- Raise blockers as soon as they appear instead of waiting for the next standup
- If your work is quiet, still post an update; a short status note is enough

## Quick Reference

New hires can remember the rhythm this way:

- `Monday`: async
- `Tuesday`: async
- `Wednesday`: live org standup
- `Thursday`: async
- `Friday`: async

If you are working on a normal day, you should either post an async update or attend the Wednesday live gathering.

# Engineering Note: Current Architecture Writeup Gate

Recent reviews showed that teams are still using the old counting heuristic to decide whether an architecture writeup is required. That heuristic is retired. Do not count repos, services, diagrams, or "number of moving pieces."

## Present Trigger

An architecture writeup is required before merge when a rollout changes both:

1. A product-owned repository, and
2. A platform-owned dependency that the product relies on in production

This is the gate even if the code change is small, even if only one team is doing the work, and even if the rollout is planned for a single release window.

In plain terms: if the rollout crosses the product/platform boundary, write it up.

## What Counts as a Platform-Owned Dependency

For this gate, a platform-owned dependency includes shared libraries, base images, SDKs, deployment templates, CI actions, service clients, data-plane integrations, and platform-managed runtime contracts that are versioned or operated outside the product repo.

## Rollout Example

A product team updates `checkout-web` to adopt a new request-signing flow. The same rollout also updates the platform-owned `@org/runtime-auth` package to change token refresh behavior and default timeout handling.

This requires an architecture writeup because the production behavior depends on coordinated changes across a product repo and a platform-owned dependency. The writeup should make the coupling explicit: version compatibility, rollout order, failure mode, rollback path, and which team owns each step.

By contrast, a product-only refactor inside `checkout-web` does not trigger this gate. A platform-only patch release to `@org/runtime-auth` also does not trigger this gate unless a product rollout must coordinate with it.

## What the Writeup Must Cover

Keep it brief. In most cases, 1 to 2 pages is enough. It must state:

- The product change
- The platform dependency change
- The reason the rollout must be coordinated
- The compatibility window, stated concretely
- The rollout order
- The rollback plan
- The product owner and platform owner

## Reviewer Checklist

Use this checklist instead of the old counting heuristic:

- Does the rollout change a product repo and a platform-owned dependency in the same production path?
- Does the note name the exact dependency, version boundary, and compatibility window?
- Does the note say who rolls out first, who verifies, and who can roll back?
- Does the note describe the user-visible or operational failure mode if one side ships without the other?

If the answer to the first question is yes, require the architecture writeup. The remaining questions determine whether the writeup is complete enough to approve.

# Company Standard for Public-Facing Product Writing

This standard applies to every piece of product text a customer can see: UI copy, onboarding, lifecycle messages, help text, settings, error messages, system notices, and marketing claims inside the product.

## The rule

Write for clarity first. Every line of public-facing product text must help a customer understand what is happening, what they can do next, and what to expect.

If a sentence does not improve understanding or action, cut it.

## Required standard

1. Use plain language.
Avoid jargon, internal terms, legalistic phrasing, and marketing filler. Prefer common words over specialized ones.

2. Be specific.
Name the action, object, limit, date, price, or outcome directly. Do not make customers guess what "it," "this," or "that" refers to.

3. Write in active voice.
Say who or what is acting. "We sent your report" is better than "Your report has been sent."

4. Lead with the point.
Put the key message in the first sentence or first clause. Customers should understand the meaning in under 5 seconds.

5. Make the next step obvious.
If action is required, state exactly what to do next in one sentence. Use direct verbs such as "Retry," "Update payment method," or "Contact support."

6. Match the message to the moment.
Success copy should confirm outcome. Error copy should explain the problem, impact, and next step. Empty states should explain value and how to get started.

7. Keep the tone calm and respectful.
Be human, not cute. Do not joke in error states, security notices, billing messages, or account issues.

8. Make claims customers can verify.
Do not use "best," "fastest," "seamless," "instant," or similar claims unless the claim is provably true in that context.

## Style rules

- Use sentence case for headings, buttons, labels, and messages.
- Use the second person: "you" and "your."
- Prefer present tense unless a time change matters.
- Use contractions when they sound natural.
- Keep UI text to 20 words or fewer when possible.
- Keep error messages to 35 words or fewer when possible.
- Use numerals for numbers 10 and above, time limits, prices, dates, percentages, and product limits.
- Write exact dates when timing matters: "July 31, 2026," not "soon."

## What good looks like

Instead of: "Your request could not be processed at this time."
Write: "We couldn't process your payment. Try a different card or contact your bank."

Instead of: "Experience seamless collaboration across teams."
Write: "Share the project with your team and assign owners in one place."

Instead of: "No data available."
Write: "You don't have any reports yet. Create a report to track usage over time."

## Review bar

Before any public-facing text ships, the reviewer must confirm yes to all five checks below:

1. Is the meaning clear on first read?
2. Is the next step obvious?
3. Are details concrete and accurate?
4. Is the tone calm, direct, and respectful?
5. Can every claim be proven?

If any answer is no, revise before launch.

# Slack Handling Plan

This is my personal operating note for a typical workweek. The goal is to keep Slack useful without letting it fragment my day. This plan is for non-urgent items only.

## Default stance

- Slack is a triage tool, not my task list.
- I do not need to answer routine messages in real time.
- If something takes more than 10 minutes to resolve, I move it into a doc, task, or calendar block.
- If a thread has gone back and forth 4 times without clarity, I switch to a short huddle or write a clearer summary.

## Daily cadence

- 9:15-9:35: first pass. Clear overnight items, scan leadership and growth channels, reply only where a same-day answer matters.
- 12:30-12:50: second pass. Handle decisions, unblock requests, and mark anything deeper for later.
- 4:30-5:00: final pass. Close loops, send updates, and queue follow-ups for tomorrow.

Outside those windows, Slack stays closed unless I am actively waiting on a live conversation.

## Response expectations for myself

- Non-urgent direct messages: reply within 24 hours on weekdays.
- Channel mentions or routine asks: reply within 48 hours if I am the right owner.
- Low-value pings, vague requests, and FYIs: acknowledge only if needed; otherwise leave unread until the next pass or archive mentally.
- Anything that needs analysis, writing, or coordination across functions: convert to a task and schedule time instead of improvising in chat.

## How I triage

- Answer now if it can be resolved in 2 minutes or less.
- Flag for today if it affects this week's growth priorities, a partner dependency, or an external commitment.
- Snooze or leave for the next window if it is informational, optional, or not yet actionable.
- Move to notes or task tracker if I will need to remember it after today.

## Channel handling

- Check core work channels every weekday during the morning pass.
- Check lower-signal channels once a day, usually in the afternoon.
- Mute channels that produce more than 5 low-value notifications per day.
- Leave channels if I have not contributed or learned anything useful from them in 3 weeks.

## Writing style in Slack

- Lead with the answer in the first line.
- Use short bullets for choices, risks, or next steps.
- When asking for input, name the exact decision and the deadline.
- When I need thoughtful feedback, send a doc with context instead of a dense Slack paragraph.

## Weekly rhythm

- Monday: review open threads, outstanding asks, and messages I snoozed on Friday.
- Tuesday through Thursday: stick to the three-pass cadence and protect focus blocks.
- Friday 4:00-4:30: clean-up pass. Close dangling threads, send status notes, and snooze anything that does not deserve weekend attention.

## Boundaries

- I do not treat responsiveness as a proxy for effectiveness.
- I do not let Slack interrupt deep work blocks unless a message is clearly time-sensitive.
- I do not carry non-urgent Slack debt into the next week if a 30-minute Friday clean-up can finish it.
